title: The excess pessimism of early nuclear bomb designers - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A GPT Pro-sourced historical review argues Manhattan Project scientists forecast the technology and arms race well (Soviet bomb 1949, thermonuclear weapons, huge arsenals, city vulnerability) but systematically over-predicted the political catastrophe because they ignored endogenous institutional adaptation such as second-strike forces and mutually assured retaliation. In August 1945 Gallup found 69% of Americans called the atomic bomb a 'good thing' versus 17% bad, i.e. the insiders were more pessimistic than the public.

insights.claim: The developers of a transformative dangerous technology were, on average, more pessimistic about its political consequences than the general public was, making insider alarm a poor guide to realized outcomes.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Discount the doom forecasts of frontier-technology insiders when sizing risk premia; the base rate favors the crowd over the builders.
insights.quote: The bomb’s developers were, on average, unusually pessimistic about the political consequences of their invention, and noticeably more pessimistic than the general public.
insights.locator: So I would summarize the historical evidence

insights.claim: In August 1945 Gallup found 69% of Americans said development of the atomic bomb was a 'good thing' versus only 17% who said it was bad, while the scientists campaigning for international control regarded the public as far too complacent.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: A hard historical benchmark for the size of the expert-public sentiment gap on a new general-purpose technology.
insights.quote: In August 1945, 69% of Americans told Gallup that development of the atomic bomb was a “good thing,” versus only 17% saying it was bad.
insights.locator: There is even some contemporary evidence

themes.theme: Where the forecasts were right vs wrong

insights.claim: Manhattan Project scientists were accurate on the technical and arms-race track — they rejected a durable American nuclear monopoly (the Soviet bomb arrived in 1949) and anticipated thermonuclear weapons, huge arsenals, and extreme city vulnerability.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Technologists forecast capability diffusion well; separate their capability calls from their consequence calls when weighting expert testimony.
insights.locator: The Manhattan Project scientists were remarkably good

insights.claim: The error mode was inferring from 'a nuclear war would be catastrophic' to 'a catastrophic nuclear war is fairly likely', which underweights the endogenous response of political and military institutions — second-strike forces, command systems, crisis management, mutually assured retaliation.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Reusable filter for any tail-risk narrative: ask whether the model prices in institutional adaptation before paying up for catastrophe hedges.
insights.quote: They tended to underweight the endogenous response of political and military institutions to the catastrophe
